Dissolution is difficult when you have large pellets of the polymers instead of fine powders. I have two suggestions; one is easy, the other depends on your access to machinery and instrumentation. 
1. Melt the polymer pellets at 150°C in a vial under an inert atmosphere. At 150°C, take the vial and drop it into a container with liquid nitrogen. This process will quench the polymer and freeze it in an amorphous state below the glass transition temperature. Remove the vial and, after allowing it to warm up a bit (to avoid thermal shock in the glass vial), add hot xylene into the vial. Since the polymer is now amorphous, the extra energy to break down crystals is not needed, and the polymer easily goes into solution. If the solution is constantly agitated, there are no local concentration gradients, thus supporting dissolution. This is a general method for dissolving crystalline polymers. The time taken will be less than 20 minutes.

I say go do the mass spec techniques. It's interesting, broad, and the lab has substantial research funding, and you'll get to meet people, conduct experiments, and learn about the process of creating a research paper.

I do not mean to offend you with this statement: you probably do not *yet* have the experience to adequately judge what the principal investigator values. Everyone wants to maintain their substantial research funding. The principal investigator favors quantity over quality, but then again, your ultimate goal is to 'get published,' so what are you valuing?

The biggest advantage you gain is that ultimately, you don't have to care. Your role as an undergraduate researcher is to receive basic training on how to perform experiments and how to avoid injury in the process.

In graduate school, you need to learn how to lead and direct experiments and then write them up into research papers. In a postdoctoral position, the focus shifts more towards 'running projects,' rather than any specific incremental paper, and when you become a primary investigator, the emphasis is on managing entire programs, each consisting of many projects, each of which will lead to numerous papers and create many doctoral candidates along the way.

My advice is to enjoy every level for what it offers you, because instead of writing about the particular interesting material my lab is working on, I'm writing a research proposal this weekend instead. Then on Tuesday, I'm going to lunch with another principal investigator, and we're going to discuss the foundation for another proposal due at the same time. Then I have to convert a failed proposal into a third proposal sometime in mid-February, I think, but luckily it's really short.

My other advice is to consider doing research terms in other labs after this first experience, perhaps at an off-site research experience for undergraduates program (such as those offered through national laboratories, or similar comparative programs).

Well, alpha particles (not to mention beams of alpha particles) were pretty new back in 1911, so the researcher was looking for deflections. He knew that matter was composed of smaller components, and he had beams of these components, so he wanted to see how they interacted with the matter. There are atoms involved, in other words, and they will deflect the beams of particles. This aligns with what another scientist was doing at the time involving x-rays and atoms and how you get these spots when you shoot x-rays at matter (diffraction patterns).

Anyhow, he sets up the experiment and collects data on the other side of the metal foil. You measure at each degree, right? Well, you conduct the experiment and your important data from your calculations is at certain angles, just like you expected, but to publish you need a full dataset. So you perform the extensive angle experiments with high signal, and then someone needs to collect all the high angles where you expect zero data (because how could this thin piece of gold foil reflect a beam of particles you're firing at it) like it never even occurred to you that you could get reflections and there would be zero data; you just need the assistant to get the zeroes right.

But lo and behold, the undergraduate assistant finds data at the high angles, and the lead researcher goes back and double checks it, and that means, oh my god, the mass of atoms is not uniform in space, the mass in atoms is concentrated, and some of the alpha particles *actually collided with a significant amount of mass in the middle of it and reflected off of it oh my god this is huge.*

Let's say you are conducting a simple chemistry experiment—such as a photoluminescence experiment. You place your sample of material and select an excitation wavelength—let's say, 350 nm—and then you look for emission at higher wavelengths (lower energy), as is typical in those experiments. So you turn on the lamp and start measuring—351, 352, 353... and you observe a large signal. You're seeing the broadness of your excitation source—resulting in a significant false signal. You continue scanning, and it levels off, making it easier to detect your compound or whatever you are studying—but then as you approach 700, you notice the signal spike again as you get close to the overtone of the 350. This creates an experimental window, and you have to strategically choose your experiments to work around it.

An interesting discussion on the Fermi paradox I read was on the progression of intelligent life. This is all based on a series of assumptions, of course. The first assumption was that if life can expand comfortably, it will. Further, if it is possible to attain levels of civilization at the type II or type III scales, then those civilizations should be easily detectable: such civilizations are not all that likely to even bother with planets anymore. Dyson swarms or even star lifting are really only problems of technology scale; they aren't particularly higher tech than we are even today, so it follows you'd expect to see more stars shrouded in all but infrared light. Lastly, even if faster-than-light travel is impossible, once a civilization is rolling out and expanding powered by fusion, there's really no reason they couldn't engulf an entire galaxy in less than three million years.

Even if there are intelligent aliens within the universe, we can look at the closest galaxies and say pretty much without concern that no one seems to be doing activities like this for the last few billion years, anyway. It's such a short time and such a big space to take over a whole galaxy that you'd expect to see it somewhere. You can't hide such operations.

So a couple of things fall out of the idea. Either 1) type II/type III civilization just really isn't tenable and is not the logical continuation of our present society or 2) wow, we might really be lonely as technologically capable species...

All conjecture, of course; we don't know how likely it is to become a type III civilization, but from my perspective, it only really requires fusion energy time and political stability.
